title: India's Middle Class Borrows Faster Than Incomes as Debt Hits Record
excerpt: Household borrowing surged 36% in a year to a record 46% of GDP, while debt service climbed to about 13% of income and real pay for salaried workers rose less than 4% over three years.
body:
• Household borrowing in India surged 36% in the year through March, taking consumer debt to a record 46% of GDP, according to central bank data reported by Bloomberg.
  • About 13% of household income in the year through March 2025 went to servicing debt, up from 10%-11% for much of the previous decade, according to CLSA estimates based on official data.
  • Borrowing rose roughly four times as fast as disposable income in 2025-26, while average earnings for regular salaried workers rose less than 4% in real terms in the three years through 2025.
  • For borrowers, the cost is set to rise: economists expect another 75-100 basis points of Reserve Bank of India rate hikes in coming months, after the benchmark rate reached 5.5%.

India's consumption boom is increasingly being paid for with borrowed money. Household borrowing surged 36% in the year through March, taking consumer debt to a record 46% of gross domestic product, according to central bank data reported by Bloomberg. Borrowing is rising much faster than incomes, the report said, even as spending continues to underpin growth in the world's fastest-expanding major economy.

The strain is visible at the household level. Bloomberg reported the case of Navjot Singh, a 25-year-old restaurant worker earning 50,000 rupees a month, who borrowed for an iPhone, a PlayStation, a television, a course and a trip home. Repayments soon ate up nearly half of his paycheck, and he cut eating out and clothes, cancelled his gym membership and gave up snooker to keep up.

"Monthly installments seem convenient at first, but you don't realize how quickly you can get sucked into a cycle of repayments."

— Navjot Singh, borrower, to Bloomberg

Borrowing is outrunning pay

Figures from the Centre for Social and Economic Progress showed borrowing rose roughly four times as fast as disposable income in 2025-26, according to Bloomberg. Pay gains after inflation were modest: average earnings for regular salaried workers rose less than 4% in real terms in the three years through 2025, based on Periodic Labour Force Survey figures.

The repayment share has moved with the debt stock. About 13% of household income in the year through March 2025 was used to service debt, up from 10%-11% for much of the previous decade, according to CLSA estimates based on official data. That compares with about 8%-9% in the US, UK and China, despite households there carrying more debt relative to income. Excluding mortgage debt, CLSA estimates Indian consumers are among the most constrained in the world.

Digital lending has widened access: loans below 100,000 rupees now account for more than two-thirds of digital lenders' books, up from 55% three years ago.

Gold loans and the turn in interest rates

Borrowing against gold, which Indian families typically use as collateral in financial strain, jumped nearly 45% in the year through March, almost three times the pace of overall bank credit, according to India Ratings and Research. Last month, major non-bank lenders such as Bajaj Finance and Piramal Finance noted that distressed borrowers are taking gold loans to stay current on loans already in default elsewhere, Bloomberg reported.

The rate cycle is now turning against borrowers. The Reserve Bank of India's 5.5% benchmark rate is already among the highest in Asia after its first increase in nearly four years last month, and economists expect another 75-100 basis points of hikes in coming months, according to the report. Saurabh Mukherjea, founder of Marcellus Investment Managers, said the spending boom will "face its first big reality check when we go through a few rate hikes."

A separate warning on consumption support

Axis Bank has separately cautioned that headline consumption rests on support that may not last. Tanay Dalal, its senior vice president for economic research, told ANI that public sector spending of around 1.7 to 2% of GDP supports consumption, and that retail sales growth slowed from 10% in August to 8% in October, according to Retailers Association of India data.

Why officials are not sounding the alarm

There is little evidence so far of widespread repayment stress, Bloomberg reported. Bad-loan ratios at banks are near multi-decade lows, and lenders have shifted personal credit toward higher-income borrowers with stronger credit profiles. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said this week that robust spending is encouraging companies to invest, and pushed back on concerns that weak wage growth could weigh on demand: "I still think India's consumption story will be intact."

The question analysts are raising is about pace. "The build-up in household debt over the last few years has been rapid. The pace has been surprising and, to some extent, concerning," said Dhiraj Nim, an economist at ANZ Bank, in the Bloomberg report. CLSA's Nikhil Gupta put the longer-run risk plainly: "This cannot go on forever." What to watch next is the RBI's rate path.
